source.title: Why Do You Grok? A Theoretical Analysis of Grokking Modular Addition
source.authors: Mohamad Amin Mohamadi; Zhiyuan Li; Lei Wu; D. Sutherland

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical analyses and empirical measurements of grokking and kernel-to-rich transitions on modular addition, using methods different from the original grokking experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports kernel interpolation and sample-complexity results, but those are not rows for delayed generalization unless they directly measure the behavior in a claim version. The sample-complexity curves in Figure 1 and loss curves in Figure 4 are not separately recorded where they do not measure a named claim-version outcome.
record.test_reason: The paper is a theoretical and empirical account of grokking modular addition. It runs its own GD experiments on two-layer quadratic networks and a one-layer transformer, showing delayed generalization, its removal by small initialization, and delayed eNTK change (the lazy-to-rich transition). It adds kernel-regime lower bounds and low-ℓ∞-norm or large-margin upper bounds. These results bear directly on V1, V3 and V5, and indirectly on V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that grokking modular addition arises from a separation between early kernel-regime behaviour, which can interpolate but provably needs a constant fraction of the data to generalize, and late rich-regime behaviour. In the rich regime, weak ℓ∞ regularization or margin bias leads to low-norm solutions that generalize with O(p²) samples (regression) or Õ(p^5/3) (classification). They also note that eliminating grokking via small initialization slows final generalization.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses two-layer quadratic networks and a one-layer transformer, theoretical permutation-equivariance and generalization analyses, and empirical NTK measurements; its experiments use explicit ℓ∞ regularization and differ from the original study's experimental recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Initialization scale changes the size of the train/test gap and can remove it; smaller scales slow training. The paper also varies problem dimension p and task formulation (regression or classification).
record.problems: Empirical findings are presented mainly in figures without uncertainty estimates. The experiments are limited to modular addition and a small set of architectures. The paper notes that large population ℓ² loss does not necessarily imply large classification error for its kernel lower bound.
record.rows_left_out: No result meeting the row criteria was omitted.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks; the experiments use a fixed n per p.
Not tested. There are no circuit-level progress measures and no removal of memorizing components. The Fourier construction (Prop 3.8) is an existence proof, not a measurement of trained networks.
Non-algorithmic data (images, text, molecules); weight-norm switching.
Ungrokking below a critical dataset size, and a direct efficiency comparison of generalizing and memorizing circuits.
Not tested. A footnote notes GD did not seem to find Gromov's solution, but no result is reported.

missing.what: Best test accuracy vs training-set size for p=113–613 (1.5p^1.5 to 2p^5/3). It supports an Õ(p^5/3) sample threshold for generalization in classification, relevant to V5's critical dataset size.
Kernel-regime lower bounds: permutation-equivariant kernels need an Ω(1) fraction of the data to beat the zero predictor (Theorems 3.4, 4.3). This explains the overfitting phase.
Classification init-scale sweep. The text says decreasing init scale makes the gap between overfitting and generalization larger or smaller.

record.verdict_notes: All empirical results are figure-only, with no seeds or uncertainty. The record wrongly linked the eNTK rows to V2; they measure the lazy-to-rich transition named in V3. The record's limits_scope labels for V3 and V5 rested on untested parts, so they are moved to untested. The V7 verdict rests on grokking appearing under plain or normalized full-batch GD; the ℓ∞ regularizer is meant to emulate AdamW's implicit bias, so the evidence is indirect. Theorem rows (r21, r22) are proofs, not measurements.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks.
It measures changes in the empirical NTK, not identifiable generalizing circuits, removal of memorizing components, or continuous circuit-specific progress measures that anticipate the accuracy jump.
Initialization scale is varied on modular addition, but non-algorithmic datasets are not tested. The paper does not test a weight-norm sweep as a lazy-to-rich switch.
LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

The paper analyzes low-ℓ∞-norm generalization and reports regularized training, but does not test whether a more efficient circuit replaces memorization, or test an ‘ungrokking’ outcome below a critical dataset size.
Whether different runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm.
Whether adaptive-optimizer instabilities or floating-point limitations cause the delay.

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretically bounded population squared loss for interpolating solutions with small ℓ∞ norm.
rows.measure: population squared loss and sample complexity
rows.baseline: Kernel-regime lower bound requires an Ω(1) fraction of all data points
rows.value: Theorem 3.6 gives population loss O((p²/n)(log n + log(1/δ))) times the all-zero predictor's loss; the text states a strict separation when n = ω̃(p²) and h = Ω(p)
rows.note: This is a theoretical generalization bound under the stated small-norm interpolation condition.
rows.check: This is a theorem, not an empirical measurement. Its baseline (Theorem 3.4, kernel lower bound Ω(p³) samples) is itself a separate result.

source_check.correct: Theorem 3.6 bounds population squared loss by O((p²/n)(log³ n + (1/p)log(1/δ))) times the all-zero predictor's population squared loss, under the stated interpolation, norm and width assumptions.
source_check.locator_found: Theorem 3.6; Proposition 3.7 and its proof in Appendix E.
source_check.problem: The recorded bound replaces log³ n with log n and omits the 1/p factor on log(1/δ).

rows.subject: two-layer quadratic network
rows.operation_detail: Theoretically bounded population 0-1 error for solutions with large normalized ℓ∞ margin.
rows.measure: population 0-1 error and sample complexity

rows.value: Theorem 4.5 gives population error Õ(√(p⁵ᐟ³/n))
rows.note: The result is conditional on the normalized-margin assumption; the paper says gradient descent can eventually find a generalizing solution with enough training data.
rows.check: A theorem conditional on the normalized-margin assumption. The kernel baseline bounds ℓ2 loss, not 0-1 error, as the authors note.
